claim: Single measurements of salivary and plasmatic oxytocin are used as indicators of the physiology of the oxytocin system.
source: Single measurements of salivary and plasmatic oxytocin are used as indicators of the physiology of the oxytocin system.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a current practice in the field.

claim: There are questions about whether single measurements of salivary and plasmatic oxytocin are sufficiently stable to provide valid trait markers of the physiology of the oxytocin system.
source: However, questions remain about whether they are sufficiently stable to provide valid trait markers of the physiology of the oxytocin system, and whether salivary oxytocin can accurately index its plasmatic concentrations.
evidence: This is stated as a research question motivating the study.

claim: The findings question the use of single measurements of baseline oxytocin concentrations in saliva and plasma as valid trait markers of the physiology of the oxytocin system in humans.
source: Our findings question the use of single measurements of baseline oxytocin concentrations in saliva and plasma as valid trait markers of the physiology of the oxytocin system in humans.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the reliability analyses conducted in the study showing poor ICC and high CV values.

claim: Salivary oxytocin is a weak surrogate for plasmatic oxytocin.
source: Salivary oxytocin is a weak surrogate for plasmatic oxytocin.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the lack of correlation between salivary and plasmatic oxytocin at baseline and after administration.

claim: The increases in salivary oxytocin observed after intranasal oxytocin most likely reflect unabsorbed peptide and should not be used to predict treatment effects.
source: The increases in salivary oxytocin observed after intranasal oxytocin most likely reflect unabsorbed peptide and should not be used to predict treatment effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that intravenous oxytocin did not increase salivary oxytocin despite increasing plasmatic oxytocin.

claim: Oxytocin plays a role in human normal and impaired socio-affective behavior and cognition.
source: In the last two decades, a wave of studies have sought to investigate the role of oxytocin in human normal and impaired socio-affective behavior and cognition (Donaldson and Young, 2008; Dyball and Paterson, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Intranasal administration of exogenous oxytocin compared to placebo is used to measure psychological or neurobiological outcomes.
source: Predominantly these include: (i) the measurement of psychological or neurobiological outcomes after the intranasal administration of exogenous oxytocin compared to placebo (Leng and Ludwig, 2016)
evidence: This is described as a methodological approach in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Genetic association studies between variations in candidate genes of the oxytocin pathway and behavioral and brain phenotypes are conducted.
source: (ii) genetic association studies between variations in candidate genes of the oxytocin pathway and behavioral and brain phenotypes (Onodera et al., 2015; Verhagen et al., 2020)
evidence: This is described as a methodological approach in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Associations between single measurements of endogenous oxytocin in peripheral fluids at rest and individual differences in neurobehavioral phenotypes are assessed.
source: (iii) the assessment of associations between single measurements of the concentration of endogenous oxytocin in peripheral fluids (mainly blood and saliva) at rest (Valstad et al., 2017) and individual differences in neurobehavioral phenotypes (Crockford et al., 2014), psychiatric disorder status and/or symptom severity (Rutigliano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is described as a methodological approach in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Single measures of baseline levels of endogenous oxytocin in biological fluids of peripheral compartments can accurately index oxytocin release in the brain.
source: The first is that single measures of baseline levels of endogenous oxytocin in the biological fluids of peripheral compartments can accurately index oxytocin release in the brain (Valstad et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an assumption underlying research approaches, with citation.

claim: Single measures provide reliable estimates of baseline levels of endogenous oxytocin in plasma or saliva.
source: The second is that single measures provide reliable estimates of baseline levels of endogenous oxytocin in plasma or saliva.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption that the study investigates.

claim: Definitive answers regarding whether single measures of baseline oxytocin can index brain oxytocin release remain to be obtained.
source: Definitive answers regarding the first assumption, whether it regards baseline or evoked release following some intervention, remain to be obtained (MacLean et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Single measurements of baseline levels of endogenous oxytocin being stable is a prerequisite for them to be used as valid trait markers of the physiology of the human oxytocin system.
source: Here, we investigate the second assumption, which is a prerequisite if single measurements of baseline levels of endogenous oxytocin are to be used as a valid trait markers of the physiology of the human oxytocin system (Wang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a logical requirement, supported by citation.

claim: There is a lack of robust evidence that single measures of endogenous oxytocin in saliva and plasma at rest are stable enough to provide a valid trait marker of the activity of the oxytocin system in healthy individuals.
source: Currently, we lack robust evidence that single measures of endogenous oxytocin in saliva and plasma at rest are stable enough to provide a valid trait marker of the activity of the oxytocin system in healthy individuals.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: Previous studies have claimed within-individual stability of baseline plasmatic and salivary concentrations of oxytocin in both adults and children based on moderate-to-strong correlations.
source: Indeed, previous studies have claimed within-individual stability of baseline plasmatic and salivary concentrations of oxytocin in both adults and children based on moderate-to-strong correlations between salivary and plasmatic oxytocin concentrations measured repeatedly within the same individual over time using ELISA in unextracted samples (Feldman et al., 2013; Schneiderman et al., 2012; Gordon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: Measuring oxytocin in unextracted samples has been postulated as potentially erroneous, given the high risk of contamination with immunoreactive products other than oxytocin.
source: First, measuring oxytocin in unextracted samples has been postulated as potentially erroneous, given the high risk of contamination with immunoreactive products other than oxytocin (Szeto et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a methodological concern raised in the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Non-oxytocin immunoreactive products might constitute highly stable plasma housekeeping proteins.
source: It is conceivable that these non-oxytocin immunoreactive products might constitute highly stable plasma housekeeping proteins (Zhu et al., 2019), which masked the true variability in oxytocin concentrations.
evidence: This is a speculation about what might explain previous findings, supported by citation.

claim: A simple correlation analysis cannot provide information about the absolute agreement of two sets of measurements.
source: Second, a simple correlation analysis cannot provide information about the absolute agreement of two sets of measurements – which would be a more appropriate approach to study within-subject reliability/stability.
evidence: This is a methodological critique based on statistical principles.

claim: It is not clear whether findings of oxytocin stability generalize beyond the early parenting or early romantic periods.
source: Third, it is not clear whether these findings generalize beyond the early parenting (Feldman et al., 2013) or early romantic (Schneiderman et al., 2012) periods participants were in when the studies were conducted, since these periods engage the activity of the oxytocin system in particular ways (Gordon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a limitation of previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Plasma and saliva levels of oxytocin are frequently altered during neuropsychiatric illness.
source: Such evidence is urgently required, given reports that plasma and saliva levels of oxytocin are frequently altered during neuropsychiatric illness and that they co-vary with clinical aspects of disease (Rutigliano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Plasma and saliva levels of oxytocin co-vary with clinical aspects of disease.
source: Such evidence is urgently required, given reports that plasma and saliva levels of oxytocin are frequently altered during neuropsychiatric illness and that they co-vary with clinical aspects of disease (Rutigliano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: The measurement of salivary oxytocin has been proposed as a surrogate for blood plasma levels.
source: The measurement of salivary oxytocin has been proposed as a surrogate for blood plasma levels (Valstad et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a proposal in the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Compared to blood sampling, saliva collection presents several logistical and measurement advantages.
source: Compared to blood sampling, saliva collection presents several logistical and measurement advantages (i.e. relatively clean matrix) (Gröschl, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of saliva sampling, supported by citation.

claim: The validity of using salivary oxytocin as a surrogate for blood plasma levels remains unclear.
source: However, the validity of this approach remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Elevations in plasmatic oxytocin after intranasal administration are likely to result from capillary absorption in the nasal cavity.
source: While elevations in plasmatic oxytocin after intranasal administration are likely to result from capillary absorption in the nasal cavity (Gossen et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated as a likely mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: Elevations in saliva oxytocin after intranasal administration could result from mucociliary clearance of intranasally delivered oxytocin from the nasal cavity to the oropharynx ('drip-down' oxytocin).
source: elevations in saliva oxytocin could result from mucociliary clearance of intranasally delivered oxytocin from the nasal cavity to the oropharynx ('drip-down' oxytocin) (Huffmeijer et al., 2012; van Ijzendoorn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a possible mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: In a previous study using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, the administration of low and medium doses of intranasal oxytocin (8 and 24 IU) elevated oxytocin concentrations in saliva.
source: In a previous study using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, the administration of low and medium doses of intranasal oxytocin (8 and 24 IU) elevated oxytocin concentrations in saliva, but the administration of a low dose (1 IU) intravenously had no effect.
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings.

claim: The administration of a low dose (1 IU) of oxytocin intravenously had no effect on salivary oxytocin concentrations.
source: In a previous study using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, the administration of low and medium doses of intranasal oxytocin (8 and 24 IU) elevated oxytocin concentrations in saliva, but the administration of a low dose (1 IU) intravenously had no effect.
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings.

claim: Concentrations of oxytocin in plasma and saliva did not correlate at baseline or after the administration of exogenous oxytocin for either route in a previous study.
source: Moreover, concentrations of oxytocin in plasma and saliva did not correlate at baseline or after the administration of exogenous oxytocin for either route (Quintana et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: Radioimmunoassay is currently the gold-standard for oxytocin quantification.
source: However, questions remain about whether the same results would have been achieved by using a more sensitive method of quantification, such as radioimmunoassay (currently the gold-standard for oxytocin quantification [McCullough et al., 2013])
evidence: This is stated as a methodological standard, supported by citation.

claim: No significant differences in mean concentration of baseline oxytocin in saliva or plasma samples were identified across the four visits of dataset A.
source: We did not identify any significant differences in mean concentration of baseline oxytocin in saliva or plasma samples across the four visits of dataset A (Plasma: F(1.47, 22.04) = 0.51, p=0.55; Saliva: F(1.06, 12.82) = 0.88, p=0.38) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: No differences in mean concentrations of baseline oxytocin in plasma were observed across the two visits of dataset B.
source: We also did not observe any differences in mean concentrations of baseline oxytocin in plasma across the two visits of dataset B (T(19) = 0.63, p=0.54).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The levels of baseline salivary and plasmatic oxytocin fluctuated considerably from one visit to another in most individuals.
source: However, in a quick inspection of Figure 1, we can observe that the levels of baseline salivary and plasmatic oxytocin fluctuated considerably from one visit to another in most individuals (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an observation from visual inspection of the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) of single oxytocin measurements in saliva in dataset A was estimated to be 0.23.
source: We estimated the intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) of single oxytocin measurements in saliva to be 0.23 and in plasma 0.29.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the reliability analysis.

claim: The intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) of single oxytocin measurements in plasma in dataset A was estimated to be 0.29.
source: We estimated the intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) of single oxytocin measurements in saliva to be 0.23 and in plasma 0.29.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the reliability analysis.

claim: The mean coefficient of variation (CV) was 63% for saliva measurements in dataset A.
source: The mean coefficient of variation (CV) was 63% for saliva and 57% for plasma measurements.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the reliability analysis.

claim: The mean coefficient of variation (CV) was 57% for plasma measurements in dataset A.
source: The mean coefficient of variation (CV) was 63% for saliva and 57% for plasma measurements.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the reliability analysis.

claim: The number of measurements required to achieve good reliability (ICC = 0.80) of a putative averaged measure was estimated to be 13.39 for saliva in dataset A.
source: We estimated the number of measurements that would have been required to achieve good reliability (ICC = 0.80) of a putative averaged measure to be 13.39 for saliva and 9.79 for plasma (Table 1).
evidence: This is calculated using the Spearman-Brown prediction formula based on the initial reliability estimates.

claim: The number of measurements required to achieve good reliability (ICC = 0.80) of a putative averaged measure was estimated to be 9.79 for plasma in dataset A.
source: We estimated the number of measurements that would have been required to achieve good reliability (ICC = 0.80) of a putative averaged measure to be 13.39 for saliva and 9.79 for plasma (Table 1).
evidence: This is calculated using the Spearman-Brown prediction formula based on the initial reliability estimates.

claim: For plasma in dataset A, higher estimates of ICC were found for visits 1-2 (0.80) and visits 3-4 (0.66).
source: For plasma, we found higher estimates of ICC for the following pairs: visits 1–2: 0.80 and visits 3–4: 0.66 (Supplementary file 1 – Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from pairwise reliability analysis.

claim: The CVs for plasma in dataset A were 31% for visits 1-2 and 45% for visits 3-4.
source: The CVs were 31% for visits 1–2% and 45% for visits 3–4.
evidence: This is a statistical result from pairwise reliability analysis.

claim: For saliva in dataset A, higher estimates of ICC were found only for the pair visits 2-3 (0.82).
source: For saliva, we only found higher estimates of ICC for the pair visits 2–3: 0.82 (Supplementary file 1 – Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from pairwise reliability analysis.

claim: Poor reliabilities were found for both salivary and plasmatic oxytocin in a subset of the sample where two consecutive samples were collected with an exact gap of 7 days.
source: In line with our main analysis, we found poor reliabilities for both salivary and plasmatic oxytocin in a subset of our sample where two consecutive saliva and plasma samples were collected with an exact gap of 7 days.
evidence: This is a result from a sensitivity analysis controlling for time interval.

claim: For both plasma and saliva in the 7-day interval subset, the estimated ICCs were not significantly different from 0.
source: For both plasma and saliva, the estimated ICCs were not significantly different from 0 and the CVs were 40% and 49%, respectively (Supplementary file 1 – Table 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: The CVs for the 7-day interval subset were 40% for plasma and 49% for saliva.
source: For both plasma and saliva, the estimated ICCs were not significantly different from 0 and the CVs were 40% and 49%, respectively (Supplementary file 1 – Table 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: Variance in the within-subject intervals between samples did not correlate with within-participant variance in oxytocin concentrations across participants for plasma.
source: Variance in the within-subject intervals between samples did not correlate with within-participant variance in oxytocin concentrations across participants neither for plasma (Spearman Rho = 0.406, p=0.118) or saliva (Spearman Rho = −0.524, p=0.065).
evidence: This is a statistical result testing the relationship between time interval and oxytocin variance.

claim: Variance in the within-subject intervals between samples did not correlate with within-participant variance in oxytocin concentrations across participants for saliva.
source: Variance in the within-subject intervals between samples did not correlate with within-participant variance in oxytocin concentrations across participants neither for plasma (Spearman Rho = 0.406, p=0.118) or saliva (Spearman Rho = −0.524, p=0.065).
evidence: This is a statistical result testing the relationship between time interval and oxytocin variance.

claim: The within-visit ICC for plasmatic oxytocin in the placebo session was estimated to be excellent at 0.92.
source: We estimated the within-visit ICC to be excellent 0.92 and the CV to be 20% in the placebo session (Supplementary file 1 – Table 3).
evidence: This is a statistical result from within-visit reliability analysis.

claim: The within-visit CV for plasmatic oxytocin in the placebo session was 20%.
source: We estimated the within-visit ICC to be excellent 0.92 and the CV to be 20% in the placebo session (Supplementary file 1 – Table 3).
evidence: This is a statistical result from within-visit reliability analysis.

claim: The ICC for single measurements of baseline plasmatic oxytocin across the two visits in dataset B was estimated to be 0.49.
source: We estimated the ICC to be 0.49 for single measurements of baseline plasmatic oxytocin across the two visits.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the reliability analysis of dataset B.

claim: The mean CV for baseline plasmatic oxytocin in dataset B was 42%.
source: The mean CV was 42%.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the reliability analysis of dataset B.

claim: The number of measures required to achieve good reliability of a putative averaged measure in dataset B was estimated to be 4.16.
source: The number of measures that would have been required to achieve good reliability of a putative averaged measure was estimated to be 4.16 (Table 1).
evidence: This is calculated using the Spearman-Brown prediction formula based on the initial reliability estimates.

claim: A significant treatment × time interaction was found for salivary oxytocin (F(3, 36) = 18.29, p<0.001).
source: For salivary oxytocin, we found a significant treatment × time interaction (F(3, 36) = 18.29, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the two-way ANOVA.

claim: The administration of oxytocin by intranasal spray resulted in significant increases of salivary oxytocin levels from baseline (t(12) = 7.06, adjusted p<0.001).
source: Post-hoc analyses revealed that the administration of oxytocin either by intranasal spray or nebuliser, but not the administration of intravenous oxytocin or placebo, resulted in significant increases of salivary oxytocin levels from baseline (Baseline vs Post-administration: Spray – t(12) = 7.06, adjusted p<0.001; Nebuliser - t(12) = 7.61, adjusted p<0.001; Intravenous - t(12) = 0.07, adjusted p=0.99; Placebo - t(12) = 0.15, adjusted p=0.99) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis following the significant interaction.

claim: The administration of oxytocin by nebuliser resulted in significant increases of salivary oxytocin levels from baseline (t(12) = 7.61, adjusted p<0.001).
source: Post-hoc analyses revealed that the administration of oxytocin either by intranasal spray or nebuliser, but not the administration of intravenous oxytocin or placebo, resulted in significant increases of salivary oxytocin levels from baseline (Baseline vs Post-administration: Spray – t(12) = 7.06, adjusted p<0.001; Nebuliser - t(12) = 7.61, adjusted p<0.001; Intravenous - t(12) = 0.07, adjusted p=0.99; Placebo - t(12) = 0.15, adjusted p=0.99) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis following the significant interaction.

claim: The administration of intravenous oxytocin did not result in significant increases of salivary oxytocin levels from baseline (t(12) = 0.07, adjusted p=0.99).
source: Post-hoc analyses revealed that the administration of oxytocin either by intranasal spray or nebuliser, but not the administration of intravenous oxytocin or placebo, resulted in significant increases of salivary oxytocin levels from baseline (Baseline vs Post-administration: Spray – t(12) = 7.06, adjusted p<0.001; Nebuliser - t(12) = 7.61, adjusted p<0.001; Intravenous - t(12) = 0.07, adjusted p=0.99; Placebo - t(12) = 0.15, adjusted p=0.99) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis following the significant interaction.

claim: The administration of placebo did not result in significant increases of salivary oxytocin levels from baseline (t(12) = 0.15, adjusted p=0.99).
source: Post-hoc analyses revealed that the administration of oxytocin either by intranasal spray or nebuliser, but not the administration of intravenous oxytocin or placebo, resulted in significant increases of salivary oxytocin levels from baseline (Baseline vs Post-administration: Spray – t(12) = 7.06, adjusted p<0.001; Nebuliser - t(12) = 7.61, adjusted p<0.001; Intravenous - t(12) = 0.07, adjusted p=0.99; Placebo - t(12) = 0.15, adjusted p=0.99) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis following the significant interaction.

claim: A significant time × treatment interaction was found for plasmatic oxytocin (F(3, 45) = 3.99, p=0.02).
source: For plasmatic oxytocin, we found a significant time × treatment interaction (F(3, 45) = 3.99, p=0.02).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the two-way ANOVA.

claim: The intravenous administration of oxytocin resulted in a significant increase in plasmatic oxytocin (t(15) = 3.73, adjusted p=0.001).
source: Post-hoc investigations revealed that the intravenous administration of oxytocin resulted in a significant increase in plasmatic oxytocin, but placebo or intranasal administration of oxytocin using either the spray or the nebuliser did not produce any changes from baseline at this time-point (Baseline vs Post-administration: Spray – t(15) = 1.38, adjusted p=0.52; Nebuliser - t(15) = 0.25, adjusted p=0.99; Intravenous - t(15) = 3.73, adjusted p=0.001; Placebo - t(15) = 1.54, adjusted p=0.41) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis following the significant interaction.

claim: Intranasal administration of oxytocin using spray did not produce changes in plasmatic oxytocin from baseline at 115 min post-administration (t(15) = 1.38, adjusted p=0.52).
source: Post-hoc investigations revealed that the intravenous administration of oxytocin resulted in a significant increase in plasmatic oxytocin, but placebo or intranasal administration of oxytocin using either the spray or the nebuliser did not produce any changes from baseline at this time-point (Baseline vs Post-administration: Spray – t(15) = 1.38, adjusted p=0.52; Nebuliser - t(15) = 0.25, adjusted p=0.99; Intravenous - t(15) = 3.73, adjusted p=0.001; Placebo - t(15) = 1.54, adjusted p=0.41) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis following the significant interaction.

claim: Intranasal administration of oxytocin using nebuliser did not produce changes in plasmatic oxytocin from baseline at 115 min post-administration (t(15) = 0.25, adjusted p=0.99).
source: Post-hoc investigations revealed that the intravenous administration of oxytocin resulted in a significant increase in plasmatic oxytocin, but placebo or intranasal administration of oxytocin using either the spray or the nebuliser did not produce any changes from baseline at this time-point (Baseline vs Post-administration: Spray – t(15) = 1.38, adjusted p=0.52; Nebuliser - t(15) = 0.25, adjusted p=0.99; Intravenous - t(15) = 3.73, adjusted p=0.001; Placebo - t(15) = 1.54, adjusted p=0.41) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis following the significant interaction.

claim: Placebo administration did not produce changes in plasmatic oxytocin from baseline at 115 min post-administration (t(15) = 1.54, adjusted p=0.41).
source: Post-hoc investigations revealed that the intravenous administration of oxytocin resulted in a significant increase in plasmatic oxytocin, but placebo or intranasal administration of oxytocin using either the spray or the nebuliser did not produce any changes from baseline at this time-point (Baseline vs Post-administration: Spray – t(15) = 1.38, adjusted p=0.52; Nebuliser - t(15) = 0.25, adjusted p=0.99; Intravenous - t(15) = 3.73, adjusted p=0.001; Placebo - t(15) = 1.54, adjusted p=0.41) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis following the significant interaction.

claim: No significant correlation was found between oxytocin concentrations measured in saliva and plasma at baseline (r = 0.10, Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.23,0.37], p=0.18, BF = 3.02, N = 63).
source: We did not find a significant correlation between oxytocin concentrations measured in saliva and plasma at baseline (r = 0.10 – Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.23,0.37], p=0.18, BF = 3.02, N = 63) (Figure 3)
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: No significant correlation was found between salivary and plasmatic oxytocin following the administration of exogenous oxytocin by spray (r = −0.21, Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.64,0.32], p=0.43, BF = 2.43, N = 16).
source: or following the administration of exogenous oxytocin (spray: r = −0.21 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.64,0.32], p=0.43, BF = 2.43, N = 16; nebuliser: r = 0.07 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.45, 0.57], p=0.65, BF = 3.32, N = 14; intravenous: r = −0.05 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.52, 0.43], p=0.84, BF = 3.27, N = 17; placebo: r = −0.20 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.64, 0.32], p=0.45, BF = 2.48, N = 16) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: No significant correlation was found between salivary and plasmatic oxytocin following the administration of exogenous oxytocin by nebuliser (r = 0.07, Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.45, 0.57], p=0.65, BF = 3.32, N = 14).
source: or following the administration of exogenous oxytocin (spray: r = −0.21 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.64,0.32], p=0.43, BF = 2.43, N = 16; nebuliser: r = 0.07 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.45, 0.57], p=0.65, BF = 3.32, N = 14; intravenous: r = −0.05 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.52, 0.43], p=0.84, BF = 3.27, N = 17; placebo: r = −0.20 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.64, 0.32], p=0.45, BF = 2.48, N = 16) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: No significant correlation was found between salivary and plasmatic oxytocin following the intravenous administration of exogenous oxytocin (r = −0.05, Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.52, 0.43], p=0.84, BF = 3.27, N = 17).
source: or following the administration of exogenous oxytocin (spray: r = −0.21 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.64,0.32], p=0.43, BF = 2.43, N = 16; nebuliser: r = 0.07 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.45, 0.57], p=0.65, BF = 3.32, N = 14; intravenous: r = −0.05 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.52, 0.43], p=0.84, BF = 3.27, N = 17; placebo: r = −0.20 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.64, 0.32], p=0.45, BF = 2.48, N = 16) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: No significant correlation was found between salivary and plasmatic oxytocin following placebo administration (r = −0.20, Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.64, 0.32], p=0.45, BF = 2.48, N = 16).
source: or following the administration of exogenous oxytocin (spray: r = −0.21 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.64,0.32], p=0.43, BF = 2.43, N = 16; nebuliser: r = 0.07 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.45, 0.57], p=0.65, BF = 3.32, N = 14; intravenous: r = −0.05 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.52, 0.43], p=0.84, BF = 3.27, N = 17; placebo: r = −0.20 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.64, 0.32], p=0.45, BF = 2.48, N = 16) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: Changes in oxytocin concentrations from baseline to post-administration did not correlate between saliva and plasma in any of the treatment conditions.
source: Changes in oxytocin concentrations from baseline to post-administration also did not correlate between saliva and plasma, in any of our treatment conditions (spray: r = 0.134 – Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.25,0.67], p=0.62, BF = 4.68, N = 16; nebuliser: r = 0.10 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.50, 0.45], p=0.73, BF = 4.71, N = 14; intravenous: r = 0.08 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.36, 0.68], p=0.76, BF = 5.19, N = 17; placebo: r = −0.16 Bootstrap 95% CI [−0.39, 0.27], p=0.56, BF = 4.47, N = 16).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis of change scores.

claim: The poor reliability indexes for single measurements of baseline oxytocin in both plasma and saliva suggest that single measures cannot be consistently measured for the same individual across different days.
source: We reported poor reliability indexes for single measurements of baseline oxytocin in both plasma and saliva. This suggests that single measures of baseline oxytocin in either fluid cannot be consistently measured for the same individual across different days.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reliability data.

claim: The reliability estimates found in the current study are in the range of those already described for other hypothalamic hormones such as vasopressin and prolactin.
source: The reliability estimates found in the current study are in the range of those already described for other hypothalamic hormones such as vasopressin (Quintana et al., 2017) or prolactin (Muti et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: The poor reliabilities are unlikely to be explained by variability in the time-interval between visits of the same individual.
source: These poor reliabilities are unlikely to be explained by variability in the time-interval between visits of the same individual.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence from the study.

claim: The mean CV for baseline concentrations of oxytocin in saliva and plasma is higher than four times the intra-assay variability of the radioimmunoassay used (<10%).
source: We note that the mean CV for baseline concentrations of oxytocin in saliva and plasma is higher than four times the intra-assay variability of the radioimmunoassay we used (<10%).
evidence: This is a comparison between the observed variability and the assay's technical variability.

claim: The low reliability of endogenous oxytocin measurements across visits results from true intrinsic individual biological variability and not technical variability/error in the method used for oxytocin quantification.
source: Together, this suggests that the low reliability of endogenous oxytocin measurements across visits in the current study results from true intrinsic individual biological variability and not technical variability/error in the method used for oxytocin quantification.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of within-session and between-session variability and the assay's technical characteristics.

claim: Several factors might underlie the intra-individual biological variability in plasmatic and salivary oxytocin, including differences in sexual activity, perceived stress, amount of social interactions, or other non-acknowledged biological rhythms.
source: These include differences across participants in sexual activity in the days preceding each visit, perceived stress, the amount of social interactions, or other non-acknowledged biological rhythms conditioning variations in oxytocin secretion throughout time (Jong et al., 2015; Engel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation about potential sources of variability, supported by citations.

claim: Oxytocin is secreted in a pulsatile manner in healthy males even at rest.
source: For instance, one study showed that oxytocin is secreted in a pulsatile manner in healthy males even at rest (Baskaran et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: Sampling during different phases of the pulsatile release of oxytocin for plasma across sessions could explain the discrepancies in oxytocin measurements observed across visits.
source: Therefore, sampling during different phases of the pulsatile release of oxytocin for plasma across sessions could explain the discrepancies in oxytocin measurements observed in the current study across visits.
evidence: This is a speculation about a mechanism that could explain the observed variability.

claim: The time-interval between measurements does not seem to significantly impact on the reliability of baseline oxytocin.
source: The time-interval between measurements do not seem to significantly impact on the reliability of baseline oxytocin, as suggested by the overlap of the 95% confidence intervals of the ICCs estimated for each pair of sessions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis of ICCs across different time intervals.

claim: The observation of poor reliability questions the use of single measurements of baseline oxytocin concentrations in saliva and plasma as valid trait markers of the physiology of the oxytocin system in humans.
source: Our observation of poor reliability questions the use of single measurements of baseline oxytocin concentrations in saliva and plasma as valid trait markers of the physiology of the oxytocin system in humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the reliability findings.

claim: Single measurements of baseline oxytocin can, at best, provide reliable state markers within short time-intervals (5 min in the study).
source: Instead, we suggest that, at best, these measurements can provide reliable state markers within short time-intervals (5 min in our study).
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the within-session reliability findings.

claim: The data does not support previous claims of high stability of plasmatic and salivary oxytocin within individuals over time.
source: Our data does not support previous claims of high stability of plasmatic and salivary oxytocin within individuals over time.
evidence: This is a conclusion that contradicts previous findings.

claim: Feldman et al., 2013 assessed plasmatic oxytocin in recent mothers and fathers at two time-points spaced 6 months apart during the postpartum period and found strong correlations between the two assessments.
source: For instance, in one study, Feldman et al., 2013 assessed plasmatic oxytocin in recent mothers and fathers at two time-points spaced 6 months apart during the postpartum period. The authors found strong correlations between the two assessments for both mothers and fathers (Feldman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: Schneiderman et al., 2012 found strong correlations between plasmatic oxytocin concentrations measured at two different instances spaced 6 months apart in both single and individuals recently involved in a new romantic relationship.
source: In another study, Schneiderman et al., 2012 found strong correlations between plasmatic oxytocin concentrations measured at two different instances spaced 6 months apart in both single and individuals recently involved in a new romantic relationship (Schneiderman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: Previous studies by Feldman et al. and Schneiderman et al. used ELISA without extraction, reporting concentrations of plasmatic oxytocin well above the typical physiological range of 1–10 pg/ml detected in extracted samples.
source: Regarding the first difference, these previous studies used ELISA without extraction, reporting concentrations of plasmatic oxytocin well above the typical physiological range of 1–10 pg/ml detected in extracted samples (in their studies, the authors report concentrations above 200 pg/ml).
evidence: This is a methodological critique of previous studies.

claim: The inclusion of extraction has been postulated as a critical step for obtaining valid measures of oxytocin in biological fluids.
source: The inclusion of extraction has been postulated as a critical step for obtaining valid measures of oxytocin in biological fluids (Szeto et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a methodological principle from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Unextracted samples were shown to contain immunoreactive products other than oxytocin.
source: Unextracted samples were shown to contain immunoreactive products other than oxytocin (Szeto et al., 2011), which contribute largely to the concentrations of oxytocin estimated by this method.
evidence: This is a finding from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: It is possible that non-oxytocin products in unextracted samples might represent highly stable plasma housekeeping molecules that masked the true biological variability in oxytocin concentrations in previous studies.
source: It is possible that these non-oxytocin products might represent highly stable plasma housekeeping molecules (Zhu et al., 2019) that masked the true biological variability in oxytocin concentrations between assessments in these previous studies that we could detect in extracted samples in our study.
evidence: This is a speculation about why previous studies found different results, supported by citation.

claim: The current study used a normative sample that did not specify inclusion criteria related to early parenting or romantic periods.
source: Instead, we used a normative sample that did not specify these inclusion criteria.
evidence: This is a description of the study's sample characteristics.

claim: The study's estimates of reliability are a better starter point for studies where specific circumstances potentially affecting the activity of the oxytocin system have not been specified a priori.
source: Hence, our estimates of reliability are a better starter point for all studies where specific circumstances potentially affecting the activity of the oxytocin system have not been specified a priori.
evidence: This is a claim about the generalizability of the study's findings.

claim: The data poses questions about the interpretation of previous evidence seeking to associate single measurements of baseline oxytocin in saliva and plasma with individual differences in a range of neuro-behavioral or clinical traits.
source: Our data poses questions about the interpretation of previous evidence seeking to associate single measurements of baseline oxytocin in saliva and plasma with individual differences in a range of neuro-behavioral or clinical traits.
evidence: This is an implication of the study's findings for previous research.

claim: Almost all previous studies associating baseline oxytocin with traits have relied on the collection of single samples from each individual.
source: Almost all these previous studies have relied on the collection of single samples from each individual.
evidence: This is a characterization of previous research practices.

claim: The findings suggest measures of oxytocin could be inconsistent and thus it is unlikely that a single sample may accurately represent oxytocin physiology and thus capture relevant inter-individual differences.
source: Our findings suggest measures of oxytocin could be inconsistent and thus it is unlikely that a single sample may accurately represent oxytocin physiology and thus capture relevant inter-individual differences.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the reliability findings.

claim: Reliability of measurements impacts power to detect correlations against these measurements.
source: Reliability of measurements also impacts power to detect correlations against these measurements (Kanyongo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statistical principle, supported by citation.

claim: Given the less-than-perfect reliability of oxytocin measurements (ICC around 0.30), to detect small-to-medium correlations (r = 0.20–0.50), researchers would need sample sizes between 102 and 651 participants to reach minimally acceptable power (80%).
source: Given the less-than-perfect reliability of oxytocin measurements (ICC around 0.30) we show here, to detect the small-to-medium (r = 0.20–0.50) correlations typically reported in studies using these measurements (Torres et al., 2018), researchers would need sample sizes between 102 and 651 participants to reach minimally acceptable power (80%).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the reliability findings and statistical principles, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Sample sizes in association studies of endogenous oxytocin measurements are typically below 100 participants.
source: Sample sizes in association studies of endogenous oxytocin measurements are typically below 100 participants (Torres et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a characterization of typical sample sizes in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Salivary and plasmatic oxytocin did not correlate at baseline or after administration of exogenous oxytocin (irrespective of route), replicating previous observations.
source: Turning to our second main finding, salivary and plasmatic oxytocin did not correlate at baseline or after administration of exogenous oxytocin (irrespective of route), replicating previous observations of a null association between measurements in these two compartments (Javor et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of the correlation findings, noting replication of previous work.

claim: The lack of significant associations between salivary and plasmatic oxytocin was further supported through Bayesian analyses which demonstrated that given the data the null hypotheses were at least three times more likely than the alternative hypothesis.
source: The lack of significant associations between salivary and plasmatic oxytocin (and respective changes from baseline) was further supported through our Bayesian analyses which demonstrated that given our data the null hypotheses were at least three times more likely than the alternative hypothesis.
evidence: This is a statistical result from Bayesian analysis supporting the null findings.

claim: The study did not control or manipulate the rate of saliva flow.
source: First, as in all other studies in the field, we did not control or manipulate the rate of saliva flow in the current study.
evidence: This is a description of a methodological limitation.

claim: Lipid insoluble molecules, such as oxytocin, enter into saliva mainly via the tight junctions between acinar cells through ultrafiltration.
source: Lipid insoluble molecules, such as oxytocin, enter into saliva mainly via the tight junctions between acinar cells through ultrafiltration (Vining et al., 1983).
evidence: This is a description of a physiological mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: If oxytocin reaches the saliva compartment through an ultrafiltration mechanism (which depends on saliva flow rate) then it is possible that when saliva flow is stimulated, oxytocin measurements may better index its plasmatic concentrations.
source: If oxytocin does reach the saliva compartment through an ultrafiltration mechanism (which depends on saliva flow rate [Gröschl, 2008]) then it is possible that when saliva flow is stimulated, oxytocin measurements may better index its plasmatic concentrations.
evidence: This is a speculation about how methodology might affect the relationship between salivary and plasmatic oxytocin.

claim: Studies have been using increases in salivary oxytocin after the intranasal administration of exogenous oxytocin to index systemic absorption and establish putative time-windows during which neurobehavioral effects may be expected.
source: Studies have been using increases in salivary oxytocin after the intranasal administration of exogenous oxytocin to index systemic absorption and establish putative time-windows during which neurobehavioral effects of oxytocin administration may be expected.
evidence: This is a description of current research practices in the field.

claim: The study could replicate previous evidence that intravenous oxytocin does not increase salivary oxytocin.
source: We could replicate previous evidence that intravenous oxytocin does not increase salivary oxytocin (Quintana et al., 2018)
evidence: This is a replication of a previous finding, supported by citation.

claim: The lack of increase in salivary oxytocin after intravenous administration is not limited to the specific low dose of intravenous OT that was previously used (1IU).
source: and extended it by showing that the lack of increase in salivary oxytocin is not limited to the specific low dose of intravenous OT that was previously used (1IU)
evidence: This is an extension of previous findings using a higher dose.

claim: The lack of increase in salivary oxytocin after intravenous administration is not driven by the insufficient sensitivity of the OT measurement method.
source: and that it is not driven by the insufficient sensitivity of the OT measurement method which had resulted in more than 50% of the saliva samples being discarded in the previous study (Quintana et al., 2018).
evidence: This addresses a methodological limitation of previous work.

claim: The data supports the notion that increases in salivary oxytocin after its intranasal administration most likely reflect drip-down oxytocin from the nasal cavity.
source: Therefore, our data supports the notion that increases in salivary oxytocin after its intranasal administration most likely reflect drip-down oxytocin from the nasal cavity (Quintana et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results, supported by citation.

claim: If increases in salivary oxytocin after intranasal administration reflect drip-down oxytocin, then oxytocin elevations in saliva are mainly driven by non-absorbed exogenous oxytocin and therefore their use to estimate levels of systemic absorption or predict treatment effects is not valid.
source: If this is the case then oxytocin elevations in saliva are mainly driven by non-absorbed exogenous oxytocin and therefore their use to estimate levels of systemic absorption or predict treatment effects after intranasal oxytocin administration is not valid.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of the drip-down hypothesis.

claim: The drip-down phenomenon is expected to be particularly pronounced for higher administered volumes.
source: We expect this phenomenon to be particularly pronounced for higher administered volumes.
evidence: This is a speculation about factors that might affect the magnitude of the drip-down effect.

claim: The lack of increase in salivary oxytocin after the intravenous administration of exogenous oxytocin raises the question of how oxytocin reaches the saliva if not from the blood.
source: The lack of increase in salivary oxytocin after the intravenous administration of exogenous oxytocin that was consistently found in our study and in a previous study (Quintana et al., 2018) also raises the question of how oxytocin reaches the saliva if not from the blood.
evidence: This is a question raised by the findings.

claim: Currently, there is no evidence of direct acinar secretion or direct nerve terminals release of oxytocin to the saliva.
source: Currently, there is no evidence of direct acinar secretion or direct nerve terminals release of oxytocin to the saliva; therefore, transport from the blood remains as the most plausible mechanism of appearance of oxytocin in the saliva.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding mechanisms.

claim: Transport from the blood remains as the most plausible mechanism of appearance of oxytocin in the saliva.
source: Currently, there is no evidence of direct acinar secretion or direct nerve terminals release of oxytocin to the saliva; therefore, transport from the blood remains as the most plausible mechanism of appearance of oxytocin in the saliva.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of evidence for alternative mechanisms.

claim: There is a current hypothesis that salivary oxytocin might be superior to plasma in indexing central levels of oxytocin in the CSF.
source: Clarifying these mechanisms of transport is paramount, given the current hypothesis that salivary oxytocin might be superior to plasma in indexing central levels of oxytocin in the CSF (Martin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of a hypothesis in the literature, supported by citation.

claim: The peak in plasmatic oxytocin occurs immediately after the end of its intravenous administration – 115 min before the post-administration saliva sample collection.
source: While this may be possible, in a previous companion paper we showed that the peak in plasmatic oxytocin occurs immediately after the end of its intravenous administration – 115 min before our post-administration saliva sample collection (Martins et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from a companion paper, supported by citation.

claim: It is unlikely that the 115 min interval would not have captured a significant delay in saliva elevation of oxytocin if it really existed, especially when after this time-interval plasma oxytocin still remained elevated compared to baseline levels.
source: It is therefore unlikely that this large interval of time would not have captured a significant delay in saliva elevation of oxytocin if it really existed, especially when after this time-interval plasma oxytocin still remained elevated, compared to baseline levels.
evidence: This is an argument against the kinetics explanation for the lack of salivary oxytocin increase.

claim: A strength of the study is the replication of poor reliability for baseline plasmatic oxytocin in a second independent dataset.
source: A strength of our study is the replication of poor reliability for baseline plasmatic oxytocin in a second independent dataset, which strengths our confidence in the robustness of our reliability findings.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's strengths.

claim: The study only considered baseline measures in reliability analyses.
source: First, we only considered baseline measures in our reliability analyses.
evidence: This is a description of a study limitation.

claim: Stimuli-evoked release of endogenous oxytocin might present higher reliability than baseline measures.
source: As for other hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical markers where evoked measures present higher reliability than baseline measures (Coste et al., 1994), stimuli-evoked release of endogenous oxytocin (i.e. after social interaction, stress, pain) might also present higher reliability.
evidence: This is a speculation about evoked measures, supported by analogy to other hormones and citation.

claim: The study's conclusions are restricted to male participants and to the radioimmunoassay method of oxytocin measurement.
source: Our conclusions are also restricted to male participants and to the radioimmunoassay method of oxytocin measurement, precluding extrapolations to female populations or to other quantification methods.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of generalizability.

claim: Due to time and logistical constraints during MRI setup, saliva could only be sampled before administration and at the end of the scanning period.
source: Also, due to time and logistical constrains during our MRI setup, we could only sample saliva before administration and at the end of the scanning period, leaving our analyses on the effects of the administration of exogenous oxytocin on its concentration in saliva restricted to one single-time point post-administration.
evidence: This is a description of a methodological limitation.

claim: It is unlikely that peak increases in saliva oxytocin after intravenous administration were missed, given that the dose administered intravenously resulted in sustained increases in plasmatic oxytocin over the course of 2 hr.
source: This is unlikely given that the dose we administered intravenously resulted in sustained increases in plasmatic oxytocin over the course of 2 hr.
evidence: This is an argument against a potential limitation, based on the pharmacokinetics data.

claim: Previous studies have found evidence of increased salivary oxytocin after single intranasal administrations of 16IU and 24IU oxytocin up to seven hours post-administration.
source: Currently, we have no estimate for the half-life of oxytocin in saliva; however, given that previous studies have found evidence of increased salivary oxytocin after single intranasal administrations of 16IU and 24IU oxytocin up to seven hours post-administration (van Ijzendoorn et al., 2012), it is unlikely that the half-life of oxytocin is shorter in the saliva than in the plasma.
evidence: This is a summary of previous findings, supported by citation.

claim: It is unlikely that the half-life of oxytocin is shorter in the saliva than in the plasma.
source: Currently, we have no estimate for the half-life of oxytocin in saliva; however, given that previous studies have found evidence of increased salivary oxytocin after single intranasal administrations of 16IU and 24IU oxytocin up to seven hours post-administration (van Ijzendoorn et al., 2012), it is unlikely that the half-life of oxytocin is shorter in the saliva than in the plasma.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous findings about the duration of salivary oxytocin elevation.

claim: Salivary and plasmatic oxytocin should not be used interchangeably.
source: Salivary oxytocin is a weak surrogate for plasmatic oxytocin; hence, salivary and plasmatic oxytocin should not be used interchangeably.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the lack of correlation between the two measures.

claim: Increases in salivary oxytocin after intranasal oxytocin administration should not be used to predict treatment effects.
source: Finally, increases in salivary oxytocin after the intranasal administration of exogenous oxytocin most likely represent drip-down transport from the nasal to the oral cavity and not systemic absorption. Therefore, increases in salivary oxytocin after intranasal oxytocin administration should not be used to predict treatment effects.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the interpretation that salivary increases reflect drip-down rather than absorption.

claim: Dataset A included 17 healthy, right-handed, male volunteers (mean age (SD) = 23.75 (5.10); range = 18–34).
source: Dataset A included 17 healthy, right-handed, male volunteers (mean age (SD) = 23.75 (5.10); range = 18–34) who contributed samples over four visits, as part of a larger study.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: Dataset B included 20 healthy, right-handed, male volunteers (mean age (SD) = 24.8 (3.70); range = 21–37).
source: Dataset B (independent replication study) included 20 healthy, right-handed, male volunteers (mean age (SD) = 24.8 (3.70); range = 21–37), who contributed samples over two visits as part of a different study
evidence: This is a description of the replication study sample.

claim: All participants had no history of psychiatric disorders or substance abuse, scored negatively on a screening test for recreational drug use, and did not currently use any medication.
source: All participants had no history of psychiatric disorders or substance abuse, scored negatively on a screening test for recreational drug use, and did not currently use any medication.
evidence: This is a description of participant inclusion criteria.

claim: Participants were advised to avoid heavy exercise, alcohol, or smoking the day before scanning and avoid any drink or food within 2 hr before scanning.
source: Participants were advised to avoid heavy exercise, alcohol, or smoking the day before scanning and avoid any drink or food within 2 hr before scanning.
evidence: This is a description of study procedures.

claim: Both studies were approved by King's College London Research Ethics Committee.
source: Both studies were approved by King's College London Research Ethics Committee (Dataset A: PNM/13/14–163; Dataset B: PNM/14/15–32).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The sample size and number of samples collected per individual would have allowed detection of intra-class correlation coefficients (ICC) of at least 0.70 (moderate reliability) with 80% of power.
source: For both studies, our sample size and number of samples collected per individual would have allowed us to detect intra-class correlation coefficients (ICC) of at least 0.70 (moderate reliability) with 80% of power (Bujang and Baharum, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical power of the study, supported by citation.

claim: Participants in dataset A received, in counterbalanced order, over four consecutive visits spaced on average 8.80 days apart (SD 5.72; range 3–28), approximately 40IU of intranasal oxytocin, either with a nasal spray or the SINUS nebulizer, 10IU of oxytocin intravenously, or placebo.
source: Participants were recruited to participate in a double-blind, placebo-control, triple-dummy, cross-over MRI study exploring the effects of various methods of exogenous oxytocin administration on cerebral physiological responses at rest (Martins et al., 2020). Participants received, in counterbalanced order, over four consecutive visits spaced on average 8.80 days apart (SD 5.72; range 3–28), approximately 40IU of intranasal oxytocin, either with a nasal spray or the SINUS nebulizer (PARI GmbH), 10IU of oxytocin intravenously, or placebo.
evidence: This is a description of the study design for dataset A.

claim: The administration of 10IU of oxytocin intravenously produces sustained increases in the levels of plasmatic oxytocin over a 2 hr course.
source: The administration of 10IU of oxytocin intravenously produces sustained increases in the levels of plasmatic oxytocin over a 2 hr course (Martins et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from a companion paper, supported by citation.

claim: In dataset A, blood samples were collected at baseline, immediately after each treatment administration, and at six time points post-administration, with the last sample acquired at about 115 min post-administration.
source: In each visit, blood samples were collected at baseline, immediately after each treatment administration, and at six time points post-administration, with the last sample acquired when participants came out of the scanner at about 115 min post-administration (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a description of the sampling protocol.

claim: In dataset A, saliva samples were acquired at baseline and together with the last blood sample.
source: Saliva samples were acquired at baseline and together with the last blood sample.
evidence: This is a description of the sampling protocol.

claim: All visits in dataset A were conducted during the morning to avoid the potential confounding of circadian variations in oxytocin levels.
source: All visits were conducted during the morning to avoid the potential confounding of circadian variations in oxytocin levels (Amico et al., 1989; Reppert et al., 1984).
evidence: This is a description of study procedures to control for confounds, supported by citations.

claim: Each participant in dataset A was tested at approximately the same time across all four visits.
source: In addition, we also made sure that each participant was tested at approximately the same time across all four visits (all participants were tested in sessions with less than one hour difference in their onset time, except for one participant where the difference in the onset of one session compared to the other three sessions was 1.5 hr).
evidence: This is a description of study procedures to control for time-of-day effects.

claim: In dataset B, baseline blood samples were obtained 15 min before MDMA/placebo administration on two separate occasions, spaced on average 9.30 days apart (SD = 5.70 days; range: 7–31 days).
source: Participants were recruited to participate in a study examining the effects of MDMA on social cognition (Gabay et al., 2019). Briefly, baseline blood samples were obtained 15 min before MDMA/placebo administration on two separate occasions, spaced on average 9.30 days apart (SD = 5.70 days; range: 7–31 days).
evidence: This is a description of the study design for dataset B.

claim: Blood was collected in 5 ml ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid vacutainers, placed in iced water and centrifuged at 1300 × g for 10 min at 4°C within 20 min of collection.
source: Blood was collected in 5 ml ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid vacutainers (Kabe EDTA tubes 078001), placed in iced water and centrifuged at 1300 × g for 10 min at 4°C within 20 min of collection and then 0.5 ml of plasma was immediately pipetted into 2 ml Eppendorf vials.
evidence: This is a description of sample collection and processing procedures.

claim: Plasma samples were immediately stored at −80°C until analysis.
source: Samples were immediately stored −80°C until analysis.
evidence: This is a description of sample storage procedures.

claim: Saliva samples were collected using a salivette.
source: Saliva samples were collected using a salivette (Sarstedt 51.1534.500).
evidence: This is a description of sample collection procedures.

claim: Participants were instructed to place the swab from the Salivette kit in their mouth and chew it gently for 1 min to soak as much saliva as possible.
source: Participants were instructed to place the swab from the Salivette kit in their mouth and chew it gently for 1 min to soak as much saliva as possible.
evidence: This is a description of sample collection procedures.

claim: For both datasets, plasma and saliva oxytocin levels were analysed by RIAgnosis, Munich, Germany using a Radioimmunoassay (RIA).
source: For both datasets, plasma and saliva oxytocin levels were analysed by a third party (RIAgnosis, Munich, Germany) using a Radioimmunoassay (RIA), as previously described (Kagerbauer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the assay method used.

claim: Plasma samples were extracted before quantification.
source: Plasma samples were extracted before quantification.
evidence: This is a description of sample preparation procedures.

claim: Saliva samples were not extracted prior to quantification since unpublished data from RIAgnosis found no differences in oxytocin concentrations between extracted and simply evaporated saliva samples.
source: Saliva samples were not extracted prior to quantification since unpublished data from RIAgnosis found no differences in oxytocin concentrations between extracted and simply evaporated saliva samples.
evidence: This is a justification for the sample preparation procedure, based on unpublished data.

claim: RIA has been previously standardised and validated and represents the gold-standard for oxytocin measurement in biological fluids.
source: RIA has been previously standardised and validated and represents the gold-standard for oxytocin measurement in biological fluids (Kagerbauer et al., 2013; Landgraf, 1981; Landgraf and Günther, 1983; Landgraf et al., 1982a; Landgraf et al., 1983; Landgraf et al., 1982b; Martin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the validity of the assay method, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The detection limit of the RIA is in the 0.1–0.5 pg/sample range, depending on the age of the tracer.
source: The detection limit is in the 0.1–0.5 pg/sample range, depending on the age of the tracer.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the assay.

claim: Cross-reactivity of the RIA with vasopressin, ring moieties and terminal tripeptides of both oxytocin and vasopressin and a wide variety of peptides comprising 3 to 41 amino acids are <0.7% throughout.
source: Cross-reactivity with vasopressin, ring moieties and terminal tripeptides of both oxytocin and vasopressin and a wide variety of peptides comprising 3 (alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone) up to 41 (corticotrophin-releasing factor) amino acids are <0.7% throughout.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the assay's specificity.

claim: The intra- and inter-assay variabilities of the RIA are <10%.
source: The intra- and inter-assay variabilities are <10% (Kagerbauer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the assay's precision, supported by citation.

claim: Reliability refers to the reproducibility of values of a measurement in repeated trials on the same individuals.
source: Reliability refers to the reproducibility of values of a measurement in repeated trials on the same individuals (Hopkins, 2000).
evidence: This is a definition of a statistical concept, supported by citation.

claim: Absolute reliability is the degree to which repeated measurements within the same subject vary over time.
source: Absolute reliability is the degree to which repeated measurements within the same subject vary over time (Hopkins, 2000).
evidence: This is a definition of a statistical concept, supported by citation.

claim: Relative reliability is the degree to which individuals maintain their position in a sample of subjects measured over time.
source: Relative reliability is the degree to which individuals maintain their position in a sample of subjects measured over time (Hopkins, 2000).
evidence: This is a definition of a statistical concept, supported by citation.

claim: ICC was estimated in a two-way mixed model, single measures, absolute agreement.
source: ICC was estimated in a two-way mixed model, single measures, absolute agreement (Koo and Li, 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical method used, supported by citation.

claim: Only participants presenting baseline measures across all four sessions were included in the reliability analysis.
source: Only participants presenting baseline measures across all four sessions were included in the reliability analysis, as previously suggested (Cuesta Izquierdo and Fonseca Pedrero, 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the inclusion criteria for the analysis, supported by citation.

claim: All statistical analyses were conducted on log-transformed oxytocin concentrations given the deviations of these measurements from a Gaussian distribution.
source: All statistical analyses were conducted on log-transformed oxytocin concentrations given the deviations of these measurements from a Gaussian distribution.
evidence: This is a description of data transformation procedures.
